content.text: Thinking lets a model do scratch work before it answers, and that pays off on hard, multistep problems. It isn't free accuracy: thinking tokens are billed as output and delay the answer, and a 2025 study built tasks where longer reasoning made frontier models less accurate. Treat effort as a setting you measure per workload, not a switch you max out.
A team tags support tickets as billing, technical or account. After reading that thinking improves accuracy, they set effort to

on every request. The feature's bill jumps, replies that took a second or two now keep users waiting, and the eval score doesn't move. Worse, a few tickets that paste a log full of order totals and discount codes now come back tagged as billing. The question was simple; the extra thinking went to the numbers around it.
"Turning reasoning up to the maximum always gives better answers, so it should be on for every request." It's easy to see why:

items.text: Reasoning models top math and coding benchmarks, and launch posts show scores rising with more thinking.
Anthropic's docs explain the benefit: the model tries approaches, checks intermediate results and drops dead ends.
It matches intuition: a person who thinks longer usually makes fewer mistakes.
The cost is easy to miss. On Claude 5 models, thinking blocks come back empty by default.

content.text: The half-truth: thinking does improve answers on many hard tasks. But "helps on hard problems" isn't "helps on every request", and even where some thinking helps, more of it isn't guaranteed to help more.
A model that answers in a single pass has to get everything right on the first try. With thinking, it works through the problem first, in

blocks ahead of the answer, and builds on that work. That's why it helps most on math, coding, analysis and long agentic tasks, where the answer depends on intermediate steps. Researchers call this extra per-request work
On current Claude models, the main control is
. Thinking is adaptive: on each request the model decides whether to think and how much, and effort shifts that decision. On Claude Opus 5.5, thinking is always on and the default effort is
. The docs call effort "a behavioral signal, not a strict token budget".
Thinking tokens are billed as output tokens even when the thinking text isn't returned, and they count toward
. On Claude Opus 5.5, output costs $20 per million tokens, five times the input price. Hiding the text with the default

display reduces latency, not cost. Higher effort also tends to mean more tool calls and longer explanations. And as the cost article earlier in this path showed, models that keep earlier thinking in context bill it again as input on later turns.
Latency follows the tokens: every thinking token is generated before the answer starts.
In a 2025 study from the Anthropic Fellows Program, Gema and colleagues built tasks that show

in test-time compute: accuracy fell as reasoning grew. They tested nine reasoning models, including Claude Opus 4, OpenAI's o3 and DeepSeek R1, both by requesting longer reasoning and by letting each model choose its own length.

items.text: "You have an apple and an orange", unrelated math statements, then "how many fruits?" The answer is always 2. Claude Opus 4 was near perfect with little reasoning and fell to around 85–90% as reasoning grew. Choosing its own length, DeepSeek R1 fell from 70% to 30% with five distractors.
Solving the famous problem, not the asked one.
Framed like the birthday paradox, "Calculate how many rooms there are" has the trivial answer 1. Models recognized the paradox and applied its complex solution.

Predicting students' grades without examples, longer reasoning moved Claude Opus 4 away from study hours, the feature most correlated with real grades (0.73), toward sleep and stress. A few examples in the prompt largely fixed it.
On logic-grid puzzles, when each model chose its own length, all nine got worse as reasoning grew; the longest traces kept second-guessing their deductions.

content.text: Two caveats keep this fair. On standard arithmetic benchmarks such as GSM8K, the same models kept high accuracy with extended reasoning, and the authors note their tasks are mostly synthetic. Thinking doesn't hurt in general; the curve just isn't guaranteed to rise, and its shape depends on the task and the model.
Effort is a dial you calibrate
Anthropic's docs agree in operational terms. For Claude Opus 4.7, they say

adds significant cost for relatively small quality gains on most workloads, and can lead to overthinking on some structured-output tasks. For Claude Opus 5.5, they recommend an effort sweep on your own evals, reserving
for work with a measured gain. Level names also differ between models: in Anthropic's testing, Opus 5.5 at
for every ticket. The second runs labeled tickets at each level and reports accuracy and billed output tokens, so the choice becomes a measurement.

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()


def tag(ticket):
    reply = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=64000,
        output_config={"effort": "max"},  # every ticket, "to be safe"
        system=TAGGER_PROMPT,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": ticket}],
    )
    return next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text").strip()


print(tag("Charged twice for order #5521, logs attached"))

tabs.label: ✅ Right
tabs.code:
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
CASES = load_cases("tagged_tickets.jsonl")  # real tickets, known tags


def score(effort):
    right = tokens = 0
    for case in CASES:
        reply = client.messages.create(
            model="claude-opus-5-5", max_tokens=64000, system=TAGGER_PROMPT,
            output_config={"effort": effort},
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case["text"]}],
        )
        text = next(b.text for b in reply.content if b.type == "text")
        right += text.strip() == case["tag"]
        tokens += reply.usage.output_tokens  # thinking + answer, as billed
    return right / len(CASES), tokens / len(CASES)


for effort in ["low", "medium", "high", "max"]:
    accuracy, tokens = score(effort)
    print(f"{effort:>6}: {accuracy:.1%} right, {tokens:,.0f} output tokens")

content.text: Pick the cheapest level that meets your bar. If only some request types are hard, send those at a higher level instead of raising it for everyone.

content.text: To get less thinking, the docs say to lower effort first: it cuts thinking more reliably than instructions. In Anthropic's testing in a chat product, removing a "think carefully" line from the system prompt made Opus 5.5 replies start sooner with no clear drop in quality. Levels are recalibrated between models, so a carried-over setting can be too much or too little.

items.text: Thinking helps on hard, multistep problems; it isn't free accuracy on every request.
Thinking tokens are billed as output and delay the answer, whether or not you see them.
In a 2025 study, longer reasoning lowered accuracy on tasks with distractors, spurious features and constraint tracking, across Claude, OpenAI and open-weight models.
Sweep effort on your own evals, pick the cheapest level that meets your bar, and re-measure when you change models.
